newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan governor makes last appeal on US bases vote.
newsitem.headline: Japan governor makes last appeal on US bases vote.

text.p: The governor of Japan's Okinawa island appealed on Saturday to the island's 900,000 voters to take part in a referendum on U.S. military bases, saying it was their first chance to air their views directly.

The plebiscite on Sunday, the nation's first on any subject, gives residents of the southern Japanese island a chance to vent years of frustration over the concentration of U.S. military forces on the island, and is expected to deliver a resounding vote in favour of streamlining the U.S. presence.

"Despite bearing an unequal share of U.S. military bases (in Japan) for 51 years after the war, the people of Okinawa have never been asked directly whether or not they approved of them," Governor Masahide Ota told a news conference on Saturday in Naha, Okinawa's provincial capital, in a final appeal for voters to turn out in force.

In the non-binding referendum, voters will be asked to give a simple "yes" or "no" to whether they support a review of the agreement under which U.S. forces are stationed in Japan and a streamlining of U.S. military bases in the prefecture.
Anti-bases sentiment on Okinawa has been running high since the rape a year ago of a local schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen that jolted the U.S.-Japan security alliance.

Okinawa hosts 75 percent of all U.S. military bases in Japan. About half of the 47,000 U.S. military personnel in Japan are stationed in Okinawa, including an entire Marine Corps division and other personnel operating the Kadena Air Force base, a strategic U.S. air base in the Asia-Pacific region.

There are 900,000 eligible voters in this tropical island prefecture in the East China Sea, out of a population of 1.27 million. Sunday's polls open at 7.00 a.m. (2200 GMT Saturday) and close at 6.00 p.m. (0900 GMT Sunday). Results are expected by 10.00 p.m. (1300 GMT).
Japan has never held a national referendum and this is the first provincial plebiscite by any of Japan's 47 prefectures.
Although the result does not mean a closure of bases, a majority "yes" vote would give the governor a boost in his campaign for a reduction in the U.S. military presence.

Only a handful of ultra-nationalists are campaigning for a "no" vote so anti-bases sentiment is expected to prevail, with Ota's future bargaining power depending on the turnout and the percentage of the "yes" vote.
Ota himself refused to predict the turnout.

The head of an Okinawan umbrella organisation campaigning for a "yes" vote said they aimed for a 70 percent turnout. "Of those who will cast ballots, we expect about 80 percent to vote 'yes'," Seiichi Sakugawa, head of the Prefectural Referendum Promotion Council, told a separate news conference on Saturday.

The referendum is not directly linked to Ota's announced plans to seek the phased closure of all U.S. bases in Okinawa by 2015. But a strong victory for the anti-bases movement would improve his chances. He is scheduled to meet Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Tuesday.
Okinawa has become a top domestic issue for Hashimoto, who has indicated that the Okinawa vote will be a major factor in his decision whether or not to call early general elections.

The rape of the Okinawan schoolgirl last year inflamed long-standing resentment over the U.S. military presence. U.S. military authorities on Okinawa delayed handing over the suspects to Japanese police on the basis of the Status of Forces Agreement governing U.S. military personnel in Japan.
The three were later convicted by a Japanese court and are now serving up to 10 years in jail in Japan.
Soon after the rape, Ota started blocking the appropriation of private land for U.S. bases. But last month, he lost a Supreme Court decision on his land appropriation campaign.
